title: Must I Obey the Ten Commandments to Be Saved? The Question That Keeps Breaking Hearts, Dividing Churches, and Hiding the Beauty of the Gospel
paragraphs:
Must I Obey the Ten Commandments to Be Saved? The Question That Keeps Breaking Hearts, Dividing Churches, and Hiding the Beauty of the Gospel
Especially Commandment Number Four... Could Missing a Day Keep You Out of Heaven?
Imagine standing before God on the day every secret is exposed.
Now imagine hearing someone say, “You can be saved if you keep the Ten Commandments.”
But then a terrifying question emerges.
How well must I keep them?
What if I break just one?
What if I struggle with Commandment Number Four?
What if I worship on the wrong day?
What if I die before I get it right?
For countless believers, this question has quietly stolen joy, assurance, peace, and confidence in Christ.
Many believe He died and rose again.
Yet they live under a cloud of fear because someone convinced them that salvation depends on how successfully they maintain the Law.
And nowhere is this debate more intense than around the Fourth Commandment.
But before we talk about the Sabbath, we must ask a much bigger question.
Because if we get that wrong, we can spend our entire lives carrying a burden Jesus already carried to the cross.
The Apostle Paul wrote words that shook the religious world of his day:
“For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast.” (Ephesians 2:8-9)
The Greek word translated “grace” is χάρις (charis).
The Greek word translated “saved” is σεσῳσμένοι (sesōsmenoi), indicating a completed action with ongoing results.
God does not say believers are being justified by works.
He says they have been saved through faith.
The Gospel does not begin with what we do for Christ.
It begins with what Christ has done for us.
Many people quote the Ten Commandments as if they were a ladder to Heaven.
But Scripture never presents them that way.
The Law was never given as a staircase for sinners to climb into God's presence.
The Law reveals God's holiness and exposes human sinfulness.
The Law functions like a mirror.
A mirror can reveal dirt on your face.
The Law can reveal your guilt.
The Law can expose your need for a Savior.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” (Romans 3:23)
If salvation depends upon commandment-keeping, every one of us is already disqualified.
James makes this even more devastating:
“For whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point has become guilty of all of it.” (James 2:10)
If salvation comes through perfect obedience to the Law, then nobody survives.
This is where the beauty of the Gospel explodes into the darkness.
Jesus did what we could never do.
He lived the life we failed to live.
Then He died the death we deserved to die.
Not finished if you add enough commandment-keeping.
The empty tomb became Heaven's declaration that Christ accomplished what sinners never could.
So what about the Fourth Commandment?
This is where emotions often rise.
Some believers sincerely argue that observing the Sabbath remains necessary for salvation.
But Scripture consistently points us to a greater reality.
The Hebrew word for Sabbath is שַׁבָּת (Shabbat).
And the New Testament reveals that the Sabbath ultimately points to a Person.
“Come to Me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.”
The Greek word used here is ἀναπαύσω (anapausō).
The writer of Hebrews takes this even further by explaining that God's true rest is ultimately found in Christ.
Paul addresses disputes regarding special days directly:
“One person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind.” (Romans 14:5)
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say salvation depends on Sabbath observance.
Some fear that teaching salvation by grace will encourage sin.
Paul anticipated that objection two thousand years ago.
“Shall we continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means!” (Romans 6:1-2)
The believer obeys God not to become saved.
The believer obeys because he is saved.
Because he has already received love.
Because salvation has already been secured through Christ.
“God accepted you in Christ. Now walk with Him.”
Perhaps someone reading this has been exhausted.
Always wondering if one more failure will cancel God's grace.
Always wondering if they have done enough.
Not because of what you did.
Your confidence is not found in your performance.
Your confidence is found in His perfection.
Your hope is not your obedience.
Your righteousness is not your record.
Your righteousness is Christ's record credited to you through faith.
The Gospel is not that good people get saved.
The Gospel is that guilty people can be forgiven.
Failures can become sons and daughters.
That is the story of Scripture.
Again and again God takes shattered lives and rewrites them through grace.
That is why our message remains the same:
If this article helped you see the beauty of Christ more clearly, do not keep it to yourself.
Have you ever struggled with the fear that you were not doing enough to be saved?
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs.
Because one shared article can reach a wounded heart.
One testimony can strengthen a struggling believer.
One act of faithfulness can point someone to eternity.
And one Savior can change everything.
The cross was never God asking you to finish what Jesus already completed.
